title: One Up on Wall Street: How to Use What You Already Know to Make Money in the Market
author: Peter Lynch
summary: Peter Lynch made his name running Fidelity's Magellan Fund to extraordinary returns through the 1980s, and his central pitch in One Up on Wall Street is that ordinary individual investors have a real structural edge over professional Wall Street analysts, if they use it: they encounter promising companies and products in daily life — as employees, customers, or simply observant consumers — years before institutional analysts notice, and small individual investors aren't constrained by the institutional pressure to only buy 'safe,' well-covered blue-chip names. His most famous piece of advice, "invest in what you know," is more disciplined than it sounds: noticing a great product or a store you love is only step one, a reason to start researching, not a reason to buy — you still have to actually study the company's fundamentals (earnings growth, debt levels, valuation relative to growth) before putting money in. Lynch organizes companies into six categories that call for different expectations and different analysis: slow growers (large, mature, low-growth, usually good for dividends), stalwarts (large, steady growers, good for moderate gains and downside protection), fast growers (his favorite hunting ground — small, aggressive, 20-25%+ annual growth companies that can become 10-baggers, his term for a stock that returns 10x the investment), cyclicals (auto, airlines, steel — whose fortunes rise and fall with the broader economy and require good timing), turnarounds (troubled companies capable of recovering sharply if the underlying business is fixable), and asset plays (companies sitting on valuable assets like real estate or cash that the market hasn't priced in). He is deeply skeptical of macro forecasting — predicting interest rates, elections, or recessions — arguing that time spent trying to time the market is better spent researching individual companies, and that a good company bought at a reasonable price will do fine through most macro noise over the long run. Lynch emphasizes the P/E ratio relative to earnings growth rate (the seed of what became popularly known as the PEG ratio) as a quick sanity check on whether a fast grower is reasonably priced, and repeatedly warns against buying a great company at any price, since overpaying for growth is one of the most common ways individual investors damage otherwise sound stock picks. The book closes with a practical checklist for actually researching a company before buying — reading annual reports, understanding what percentage of earnings come from the core business Lynch identifies with the company's public story, tracking insider buying, and being honest about how much time you're actually willing to spend following a position, since Lynch's whole approach only works if the investor does real homework rather than just acting on a hunch.

sections.title: The Individual Investor's Edge
sections.summary: Ordinary investors encounter promising companies in daily life as consumers and employees before Wall Street notices, and aren't bound by institutional pressure to stick to safe, well-covered names — a real edge if actually used with discipline.

sections.title: Invest in What You Know — But Then Do the Homework
sections.summary: Noticing a great product is only the first step, a reason to start researching a company's fundamentals — not a reason to buy on its own.

sections.title: The Six Categories of Stocks
sections.summary: Slow growers, stalwarts, fast growers (his favorite hunting ground for 'ten-baggers'), cyclicals, turnarounds, and asset plays — each requiring a different set of expectations and analysis.

sections.title: Stalking the Tenbagger
sections.summary: How to identify small, fast-growing companies with room to keep growing for years, and the checklist of traits (reasonable P/E relative to growth, manageable debt, insider buying, a plan to keep growing) that separate real tenbaggers from hype.

sections.title: Earnings, P/E, and Reasonable Prices
sections.summary: Using the price-to-earnings ratio relative to a company's earnings growth rate as a quick sanity check — a great company bought at too high a price is still a bad investment.

sections.title: Ignoring the Macro Noise
sections.summary: Skepticism toward predicting interest rates, elections, or recessions — time is better spent researching individual companies than trying to time the broader market.

sections.title: Doing the Actual Homework
sections.summary: A practical checklist for researching a company before buying: annual reports, what share of earnings come from the core business, tracking insider buying, and being realistic about how much ongoing attention you're willing to give a position.

keyLessons: Noticing a great product or company in daily life is only a starting point for research — never a reason to buy on its own.
Sort a potential investment into one of six categories (slow grower, stalwart, fast grower, cyclical, turnaround, asset play) since each calls for different expectations.
Check a stock's P/E ratio against its earnings growth rate as a quick sanity check against overpaying for growth.
Small, aggressively growing companies with room left to grow are the most likely source of very large returns ('tenbaggers'), but need real diligence to separate from hype.
Don't try to time the market by predicting interest rates or recessions — spend that time researching individual businesses instead.
Track insider buying and understand what share of a company's earnings actually comes from its core, well-understood business.
Only invest in a company you're willing to actually keep researching over time — a stock pick without ongoing attention is closer to a lottery ticket.
Overpaying for even a genuinely great company is one of the most common ways individual investors damage their own returns.

quotes.text: Know what you own, and know why you own it.
quotes.attribution: Peter Lynch, One Up on Wall Street

quotes.text: Behind every stock is a company. Find out what it's doing.
quotes.attribution: Peter Lynch, One Up on Wall Street

quotes.text: In this business, if you're good, you're right six times out of ten. You're never going to be right nine times out of ten.
quotes.attribution: Peter Lynch, One Up on Wall Street

whoThisIsFor: Individual investors who want to pick their own stocks rather than only buy index funds, and want a disciplined framework rather than tips or hunches.
whenToReadThis: Read it before researching your first individual stock pick, and revisit the six-category framework each time you're evaluating a new company.
sourceNotes: Original synthesis from general knowledge of Lynch's well-documented investment framework (six stock categories, tenbaggers, invest-in-what-you-know discipline). No source text reproduced; 3 short verbatim quotes used, all widely cited lines from the book.
